flagged.script: The fix is one you could write yourself, because it is SQL. Features are built from dated events, like the daily spend log or the ticket log, and every one is filtered to dates on or before the snapshot. With that one condition in the join, nothing from the future can get in. Days since last spend becomes the snapshot date minus the last spend date before it. Same name, honest value. For fields that live only in the accounts table, ask whether they could have changed after the snapshot, whatever the reason. Vertical and sign-up date cannot, so they are fine, with a note. Status, tier and last-activity dates can, so they need a copy dated at the snapshot.

flagged.script: Every test advertiser's real score is loaded, and the cut-off is yours to drag. Start at 0.5, then pull it down and watch the four counts change. Three things to find. The cut-off that catches nine churners in ten, and how many advertisers it flags. The cut-off where nine flags in ten are right, and how many flags are left. And the cut-off that flags about as many advertisers as the hand rule did. You will not find one that makes precision and recall both high. That is the trade you are choosing. Try it now.

flagged.script: Both candidates clear the bar. Model A and model B each miss by about 1,700 dollars on average, and B is ahead by 58 dollars. Before you believe that, ask how much of that gap is luck. Score the same two models on a different draw of advertisers and the gap moves. Here it could plausibly sit anywhere from about 180 dollars in B's favour to about 70 in A's. That range crosses zero. On average miss, then, this is a tie. More on that check in the next lesson.

flagged.script: Models are no different. A model's score is measured on a sample too. The churn model's AUC of about 0.85 comes from 4,000 test advertisers. Draw a different set and it could land anywhere from about 0.83 to 0.86. So when the assistant says a new model is better by a hair, ask for an interval on the gap between the two, measured on the same test rows. Last lesson's 58 dollar gap between model A and model B is the example. Its interval runs from 177 dollars one way to 73 the other. Zero is inside. Call it a tie, and keep the simpler model.

You know that signature: memorising. Tuned by cross-validation on the training months, it prefers trees just two levels deep, and most of the gap closes. It lands at 0.836. The forest is in the same neighbourhood. And the weighted sum sits at 0.845. All that machinery finishes nine thousandths behind.

flagged.script: Monday morning the risk list goes out. By ten, an account manager is at your desk about one name on it. The advertiser's ID ends in 754, and the list says 73 percent. Her question is fair: why? Because the model said so is not something she can take into a call. This list comes from the weighted sum, but what follows works on any model, one that predicts who will hit their CPA goal as much as one that predicts who will leave. There are three questions to ask. What does it lean on overall? How does its answer move when one column changes? And why this advertiser? Each has a standard tool, and each tool has a limit that belongs in the same breath as the answer.

Ecommerce is lower by 1.6 points. Now the flow looks harmful. And the trouble is the one from two lessons ago: the groups were never alike. Before the launch, ecommerce was at about 60 percent and the others at about 67. Ecommerce started well behind, for reasons that have nothing to do with the flow. Comparing the groups after launch blames the flow for that old gap.

flagged.script: Could you have seen it coming? Take May. Gaming churn was about 23 percent, against a prediction of 15. But with only about 220 gaming advertisers, the measured rate carries a margin of about five and a half points. The prediction sits just outside it. Part of that miss is not about gaming: the model ran about 2 points low for everyone in May. And with six verticals checked every month, a miss like this can turn up by chance. So May is a warning: note it, look for a cause, watch the next month. In this simulation the change was written in for June only. June is different. 31 percent against 14, with the same margin. That is far outside it. It is not noise.

flagged.script: That 3 percent came from random hold outs. Now judge the same model the way it will be used: train up to a date, forecast the next 28 days, score only those. The miss is about 5 percent. The first test let the model fill gaps between days it knew; the second made it reach past the end of its data. It is module four's trap in time: there, one advertiser sat on both sides of a fold. And it is general: any forecast is tested from a past date forward, and a forecast of weekly lead volume for sales needs exactly this test. A footnote: last lesson's plain regression, the trend model for short, scored the same both ways, which you only learn by running the honest test.

flagged.script: The honest test is called backtesting, and it is a rehearsal. Pick a past date and pretend it is today. Train on nothing after it. Forecast the next 28 days. Score that against what happened. Then move on a month and repeat. Last lesson's scores came from twelve of these, because one rehearsal can be lucky. The trend model's monthly miss ranged from about 2 percent to about 3 and a half. One month alone shows nothing of that spread.

flagged.script: Why can the forecast see a leak that the weekday comparison could not? On an ordinary day, spend sits about 5 percent away from its same weekday level. It sits under 2 and a half percent away from the forecast. A 12 percent drop hides inside the first and only just clears the second. Two of its five days were flagged, and a slightly wider band would have missed it. The sharper the expectation, the smaller the problem you can see. Now the caveat. This forecast has the same form as the equation that generated the series, in a world that never changes. No false alarms is a best case. On a real series, expect more.
